name: Mahatma Gandhi
info: Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi (1869–1948) was an Indian lawyer and anti-colonial nationalist who used nonviolent resistance to lead the campaign for India's independence from British rule, and whose example later inspired movements for civil rights across the world.

facts.born: 2 October 1869 in Porbandar, a coastal town on the Kathiawar Peninsula, into a Gujarati Hindu Modh Bania family; third son of Karamchand Gandhi, dewan of Porbandar state, and Putlibai
facts.died: 30 January 1948 in Delhi, shot three times in the chest by Nathuram Godse, a Hindu nationalist, in the garden of Birla House on his way to a prayer meeting
facts.role: Barrister, called to the bar in 1891; lawyer and campaigner for Indian civil rights in South Africa, 1893–1914; leader of the Indian National Congress from 1921; resigned his Congress membership in 1934
facts.known: Nonviolent resistance (satyagraha); the campaign for Indian independence; the Salt March of 1930; the call on the British to Quit India in 1942; campaigns against untouchability; fasts as political protest; the book Hind Swaraj (1909)

t: Gandhi worked out his method of nonviolent resistance, satyagraha, during 21 years in South Africa and brought it to India in 1915.
As leader of the Indian National Congress from 1921 he turned the demand for self-rule into mass campaigns, among them the Salt March of 1930 and the Quit India movement of 1942.
India became independent in August 1947 through a partition he opposed, and he was assassinated by a Hindu nationalist on 30 January 1948.
dyk: As a law student in London Gandhi was too shy to read out his own defence of a fellow member at a committee meeting of the London Vegetarian Society, so the president had another member read it for him.
ev: Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi is born in Porbandar on the Kathiawar Peninsula
After three years in London he is called to the bar at the age of 22 and returns to India
He sails for South Africa to act as lawyer in a merchant's lawsuit and stays for 21 years
At a mass meeting in Johannesburg he adopts satyagraha, nonviolent protest, against the Transvaal's registration law
He returns to India at the request of Gopal Krishna Gokhale and joins the Indian National Congress
He leads the Salt March from Ahmedabad to Dandi to break the British salt laws
He calls on the British to Quit India and is arrested and held for two years
Nathuram Godse shoots him dead at Birla House in Delhi

sections.early:
Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi was born on 2 October 1869 in Porbandar, a coastal town on the Kathiawar Peninsula and then part of a small princely state in the Kathiawar Agency of the British Raj. His father, Karamchand Uttamchand Gandhi (1822–1885), served as dewan (chief minister) of Porbandar and from 1876 of Rajkot; his mother, Putlibai, was Karamchand's fourth wife and came from a Pranami Vaishnava family. The family were Gujarati Hindus of the Modh Bania caste. Gandhi wrote that his mother, who kept hard vows and frequent fasts, influenced him deeply, as did the stories of Shravana and King Harishchandra.

At school in Rajkot he was an average student, shy and tongue-tied, with no interest in games. In May 1883, aged 13, he was married to the 14-year-old Kasturbai Gokuldas Kapadia in an arranged marriage, according to the custom of the region. His father died in late 1885, and the couple's first child lived only a few days; four sons followed between 1888 and 1900.

After dropping out of Samaldas College, Gandhi sailed from Bombay for London on 4 September 1888 to study law, having vowed before his mother to abstain from meat, alcohol and women. The elders of his caste in Bombay excommunicated him for going. He enrolled at the Inner Temple, took classes at University College, London, sat on the executive committee of the London Vegetarian Society, and read the Bhagavad Gita with members of the Theosophical Society. He was called to the bar in June 1891, aged 22, and returned to India to learn that his mother had died while he was away.
sections.rise:
Gandhi's attempt to establish a law practice in Bombay failed, because he was psychologically unable to cross-examine witnesses, and he made a modest living in Rajkot drafting petitions. In 1893 a Muslim merchant from Kathiawar, Dada Abdullah, engaged him for a lawsuit in South Africa, and in April he sailed for the Colony of Natal. He stayed 21 years. Soon after arriving he was beaten for refusing to sit on the floor of a stagecoach and thrown off a train at Pietermaritzburg for refusing to leave the first class.

When the case ended in May 1894 he stayed to oppose a Natal bill denying Indians the vote. The bill passed, but he helped found the Natal Indian Congress that year. During the Boer War he raised 1,100 Indian volunteers as stretcher-bearers. In 1906 the Transvaal required Asians to register with fingerprints; at a mass meeting in Johannesburg on 11 September Gandhi first adopted satyagraha, urging Indians to defy the law and suffer the punishments. He had started the journal Indian Opinion in 1903 and, with Hermann Kallenbach, founded Tolstoy Farm near Johannesburg in 1910.

At the request of Gopal Krishna Gokhale he returned to India in 1915 and joined the Indian National Congress. His first major achievement came in 1917 at Champaran in Bihar, where peasants forced to grow indigo for largely Anglo-Indian planters won concessions from the authorities. In 1918 in Kheda, struck by floods and famine, he organised a pledge of non-payment of revenue; by the end of May the government relaxed the tax until the famine ended.
sections.deeds:
In Hind Swaraj (1909) Gandhi had argued that British rule survived only through the co-operation of Indians and would collapse without it. After the Rowlatt Act and the Jallianwala Bagh massacre he turned to swaraj, self-rule. He became leader of the Indian National Congress in 1921 and widened non-cooperation to swadeshi, the boycott of foreign-made goods and of British institutions and law courts. Arrested on 10 March 1922, he was tried for sedition and sentenced to six years' imprisonment; he was released in 1924.

In December 1928 he pushed through a Congress resolution demanding dominion status, and on 26 January 1930 the Congress declared India's independence. From 12 March to 6 April 1930 he and his volunteers marched 388 kilometres from Ahmedabad to Dandi to make salt in defiance of the salt laws. He was interned on 5 May, and Britain imprisoned at least 60,000 people. The Gandhi–Irwin Pact of March 1931 freed political prisoners in return for the suspension of civil disobedience, and Gandhi attended the Round Table Conference in London as sole representative of the Congress. Back in prison at Yerwada, he began a fast unto death against a separate electorate for untouchables, which ended in the compromise Poona Pact.

He opposed Indian participation in the Second World War while freedom was denied to India. In 1942 he called on the British to Quit India and urged Indians to "do or die". He was arrested and held for two years, and the British government killed over 1,000 members of the movement. He was released on 6 May 1944 because of his failing health.
sections.opponents:
Winston Churchill was a vigorous British critic. In 1931 he called it "alarming and also nauseating" to see "a seditious Middle Temple lawyer, now posing as a fakir" parleying with the Viceroy, and he later described Gandhi as a dictator and a "Hindu Mussolini". The Viceroy Archibald Wavell accused him of wishing to "overthrow British rule and influence and to establish a Hindu raj" and called him a "malignant, malevolent, exceedingly shrewd" politician.

Among Indians, Muhammad Ali Jinnah opposed satyagraha, accused Gandhi of reviving Hinduism through political activism, and led the demand for a Muslim homeland. B. R. Ambedkar, leader of the untouchables, dismissed his ideas in 1945 as loved by "blind Hindu devotees". Rabindranath Tagore and other Hindu leaders questioned his support for the Khilafat Movement, and Subhas Chandra Bose, who lacked faith in nonviolence, won the Congress presidency against Gandhi's nominee. When the Khilafat Movement collapsed in 1922, deadly religious riots returned.

His consistency has been questioned. In 1918 he tried to recruit combatants for the British war effort, which his own secretary noted raised the question of his creed of ahimsa. Ashwin Desai and Goolam Vahed argue that in South Africa he was at times a willing part of racial stereotyping of Africans, though he later opposed racism against them. After his wife's death in February 1944 he tested his vow of celibacy by sleeping beside young women, among them his grandniece Manu; family members and leading politicians criticised the experiments, and some of his staff resigned.
sections.last:
Gandhi opposed the partition of the subcontinent along religious lines and proposed that the Congress and the Muslim League attain independence together under a provisional government, leaving partition to a plebiscite in districts with a Muslim majority. Jinnah rejected this and called a Direct Action Day on 16 August 1946, which set off a mass murder of Hindus in Calcutta and retaliatory violence against Muslims across India; thousands were killed. Britain accepted partition; Stanley Wolpert states that the plan "was never approved of or accepted by Gandhi". More than half a million people were killed in religious riots as 10 to 12 million non-Muslims migrated from Pakistan into India and Muslims the other way.

He spent independence day, 15 August 1947, fasting and spinning in Calcutta and appealing for peace. His fasts are credited with stopping religious riots; the last took place in Delhi from 13 to 18 January 1948, when he was 78. At 5:17 p.m. on 30 January 1948, in the garden of Birla House on his way to a prayer meeting, Nathuram Godse, a Hindu nationalist with links to the Hindu Mahasabha and the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh, fired three bullets into his chest at close range. By some accounts he died instantly; by others, about 30 minutes later inside the house.

Over a million people joined the funeral procession to Raj Ghat, where he was cremated in accordance with Hindu tradition. After a trial of eight months, Godse and Narayan Apte were sentenced to death by hanging and six others to life imprisonment; Vinayak Damodar Savarkar was acquitted.
sections.legacy:
In post-colonial India Gandhi is considered the Father of the Nation, and during the nationalist movement he was commonly called Bapu, an endearment roughly meaning "father". The honorific Mahatma, "great-souled", first applied to him in 1914 in South Africa, is now used throughout the world. His birthday, 2 October, is a national holiday in India, Gandhi Jayanti, and is marked worldwide as the International Day of Nonviolence. Raj Ghat, where he was cremated, and Birla House, now Gandhi Smriti, are memorials, and several peace prizes carry his name.

Gandhi was not the originator of the principle of nonviolence, but he was the first to apply it in the political field on a large scale. His legacy later inspired movements for civil rights and freedom across the world: Martin Luther King Jr. used the term "soul force" in his "I Have a Dream" speech, and Nelson Mandela is among the admirers of his efforts against racism. After black South Africans gained the vote in 1994 he was proclaimed a national hero there.

He was a prolific writer. Hind Swaraj became "the intellectual blueprint" for India's independence movement, and his collected works, published by the Indian government in the 1960s, run to about 50,000 pages in about 100 volumes. Assessments differ: some writers present him as a paragon of ethical living and pacifism, others as a more complex, contradictory and evolving character. Desai and Vahed argue that his image has been reinvented since his assassination as though he had always been a saint.

summary: Trained as a barrister in London, Gandhi developed nonviolent resistance in South Africa and from 1915 led mass campaigns for Indian self-rule, among them the Salt March and Quit India. Independence came in 1947 with a partition he opposed, and he was assassinated in Delhi in January 1948.
